summary: Atheera is a research-prototype software system that watches over astronauts using the Wi-Fi already on board a station. As Wi-Fi signals cross a module, a person's breathing and movement create tiny ripples in them. Atheera reads those ripples and reports each crew member's breathing rate, activity, falls, unusual movement and rest during sleep. It shows them on a dashboard with clear alerts that include their evidence and what to do next. It needs no cameras, wearables or new sensors. It addresses the NASA challenge of creating health monitoring software for astronauts. It gathers the indicators that need nothing worn and nothing to remember, and flags when a result needs attention. Where the signal is unclear, it says "lost" instead of guessing. This matters because on long missions the crew is small and help is far away, and one missed moment, such as a fall or struggling breathing in sleep, can be serious. On public recordings, Atheera reads breathing within 0.40 breaths/min of a chest belt, recognises activity with 96% accuracy on unseen recordings, and caught all 16 held-out falls. The demo is a replay of real recorded Wi-Fi data: no live hardware and no microgravity data were used. It supports crews and flight surgeons and is not a medical device.
details:
What it does and how it works

Atheera is software that watches over astronauts using the Wi-Fi already on a station. Every Wi-Fi packet carries channel state information (CSI), which records how the signal changed on its way from sender to receiver. A chest rising and falling, or a body moving, alters that path. Atheera processes this in five steps:

  1. It takes in CSI from 52 usable subcarriers.
  2. It cleans the signal with filtering, resampling and phase correction.
  3. Four readers estimate breathing, activity and falls, unusual movement, and rest.
  4. A fusion engine applies context-aware limits (sleep, rest, active, exercise), conservative adult values that can be tuned for each crew member. It raises an alert only when a problem persists.
  5. A dashboard shows each alert with its evidence and what to do next.

Breathing comes from signal processing with Viterbi tracking and a confidence score. Activity and falls come from an ensemble of four ResNet-18 networks. Simple, inspectable rules, not a model, decide when an alert is raised.

Benefits

  • Someone is always watching, including during sleep, and the crew has to do nothing.
  • It adds no mass, power or cabling, because it uses hardware the spacecraft already has.
  • Every alert shows its evidence and how sure the system is, and the system says "lost" instead of guessing.
  • On held-out public recordings, breathing error was 0.40 breaths/min against a chest belt, activity accuracy was 96.0%, and all 16 falls were caught with 1 false alarm in 96 recordings.

Intended impact

Atheera is meant to support crews and flight surgeons on long missions, where sleep loss, injury risk and isolation are named NASA concerns. It runs beside the medical kit and does not replace it. The same idea could fit any closed habitat with Wi-Fi, such as a base or a rover. On Earth, the same fall and breathing monitoring could also help people who live alone, such as elderly people at home. It covers three of NASA's five hazards (isolation and confinement, closed environment, gravity fields).

How NASA resources shaped Atheera


We used NASA's Human Research Program pages as our requirements source. 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight set the scope: Atheera covers isolation and confinement, the closed environment and gravity fields. Risks of Human Spaceflight set what each alert is for: the sleep-loss risk gave the rest tracker, the mild-hypoxia risk gave the breathing-rate alerts (a rate, not oxygen), the injury-from-dynamic-loads risk gave the fall and unusual-movement alerts, and the behavioural-conditions risk gave the rest and activity patterns. ARCHeR tracks Artemis II crew sleep and activity with a worn device; Atheera's rest tracker answers the same question from Wi-Fi, with nothing worn. Alert levels (advisory, caution, warning, emergency) follow the ISS caution-and-warning classes. The numeric limits are set by our team and none is attributed to NASA, because the NASA pages give hazard and risk names rather than thresholds. Measured results are validated on public Wi-Fi datasets recorded on Earth.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Models and signal processing: Python 3.12, PyTorch, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn.
  • Backend: FastAPI with WebSockets and a REST API, driven by a YAML scenario replay engine.
  • Dashboard: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/Radix, TanStack Query, Three.js (React Three Fiber) and Recharts.
  • Packaging: Docker Compose, with an optional Caddy HTTPS setup.
  • Hardware: none for the demo. A live system needs a CSI-capable radio such as an Intel 5300 card or an ESP32.
  • AI assistance:
    • Claude Code (Anthropic) helped write and review code, run experiments and draft documents. Results were checked against the result files.
    • Our own ResNet-18 networks and confidence calibration were trained on public recordings.
    • The demo voice-over is SI-generated, using Microsoft neural voice "Andrew" through the open-source edge-tts library. We wrote the script, and only the narration text was sent to the service.
    • No AI-generated images or video, and no NASA logo. The demo footage is real screen recording, and the graphics are HTML and SVG.

What is creative about it

  • It turns Wi-Fi into a health sensor, so there are no cameras and nothing to wear or remember.
  • It brings wrist actigraphy (the method NASA's ARCHeR research uses) to Wi-Fi to estimate rest time.
  • It is honest about uncertainty: low-confidence readings are shown as "lost", and unclear time is never counted as rest.
  • The dashboard has a 3D station view where a module turns red at a fall, plus a guided tour and a replayable night shift.

Factors the team considered

  • Scope: the indicators were chosen from NASA's hazard and risk pages. Heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature and mood were left out because Wi-Fi cannot measure them reliably.
  • Privacy and comfort: cameras are unwelcome in crew quarters, and wearables are uncomfortable and need charging.
  • Rigour: every split holds out whole recordings. The standard benchmark's 98.3% is inflated, since 499 of its 500 test windows share recordings with training. On the stricter split the same recipe scores 91.9% and Atheera scores 96.0%.
  • False alarms: a fix for receiver gain steps cut false movements from 17.3 to 2.8 per hour.
  • Safety: Atheera does not prescribe treatment, and it is not a medical device.
  • Limits: this is a research prototype and a replay: no live hardware was used, all data comes from recordings made on Earth, and no microgravity CSI exists yet. The slow-breathing demo event is real data stretched in time. Next steps are a live stream, a metal-walled mock-up, more people and rooms, and review by flight surgeons.
